analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act rule requiring large employers to offer health coverage or pay penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have repealed the health reform law's employer coverage requirement, never left the Ways and Means Committee and received no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Affordable Care Act, employers with 50 or more full-time workers must offer health coverage or pay a tax penalty. This bill would erase that requirement, along with the related paperwork rule that makes large employers report who they cover. It was introduced in February 2013, sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Large employers — those with 50 or more full-time workers — that do not offer qualifying coverage would no longer face penalties, and all large employers would be freed from the annual reporting requirement. Supporters argued the penalties and paperwork discouraged hiring and pushed employers to cut hours.

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the tax code section that penalizes employers with 50 or more full-time employees for not offering health coverage.
Also strikes the related requirement that large employers report coverage information to the IRS, eliminating that reporting work.
The changes would take effect for months beginning after December 31, 2013.

analysis.who_pays: The repeal would remove a requirement that pushes large employers to either provide coverage or contribute penalties toward the health system. Some workers could face a greater risk of losing employer coverage offers, and the federal government would lose the penalty revenue that helps fund the law's coverage expansions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and the law's coverage financing

drawbacks.text: Removing the employer requirement eliminates the pressure that keeps large employers in the business of providing health coverage; some workers at firms that drop or scale back coverage could end up worse off or shifted onto the individual market.
The penalties the bill repeals are one of the ways the Affordable Care Act is financed, so repeal adds to the cost of the law's coverage expansions.
Supporters of keeping the mandate argue most large employers already offer coverage, so the main effect of repeal is letting non-offering firms off the hook rather than helping workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clear, direct saving to large employers that would otherwise face penalties and reporting duties. Whether workers share in that saving is uncertain: some of the penalty's cost is borne by employees through wages, but repeal also removes a safeguard that keeps large employers providing coverage. On balance, the bill's benefits flow to employers and its risks fall on workers and the health law's financing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 28, 2013 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it stayed in committee through the end of the 113th Congress in January 2015.
It had 29 cosponsors, 28 Republicans and 1 Democrat.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, large employers that do not offer coverage continued to face the mandate's penalties and reporting duties, and the coverage requirement stayed on the books for workers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large employers still face the mandate

for.name: Rep. Charles Boustany
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the employer health insurance mandate.

for.name: 29 cosponsors (28 Republicans, 1 Democrat)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Tiberi (R-OH), Barrow (D-GA), and Black (R-TN) as original introducers.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never marked it up or reported it, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican — 28 of the 29 cosponsors were Republicans, with a single Democrat (Rep. John Barrow of Georgia) — and no vote was ever held.

industries.note: The bill would end the penalties and reporting duties that fall on large employers that do not offer qualifying coverage. Some of that cost is passed to workers through wages, but repeal would also free employers from the pressure to keep providing coverage.

The employer mandate steers tens of millions of workers into employer-sponsored plans, a core market for insurers; repeal would loosen that pipeline and shift more people toward individual-market coverage instead.
